item.title: NSPP plasma-water graphene oxide
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported for the lab method (peer-reviewed). Cost, tonne-scale, and “replaces graphite” claims are Preliminary. The 1 Oct 2026 Chemical Engineering item is a recurrence of a paper accepted February 2026.

Related notes: [[guides/glossary|NSPP]] · [[topics/health/form-route|GO]] · [[reference/production]]

Five facts

  1. Banavath et al. grow graphene oxide at a methane–water interface with a non-thermal atmospheric nanosecond pulsed plasma (NSPP). No mined graphite, no Hummers acids.
  2. Journal: Nature Communications, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-69831-0. Received 9 Aug 2025, accepted 9 Feb 2026. Texas A&M plus LTEOIL (College Station).
  3. Reported lab rate: a four-gap reactor up to about 5 g GO per day. That is a bench scale-up, not a plant.
  4. Hydrogen is the co-product. The project started as a hydrogen effort; carbon sheets were the unexpected high-value solid.
  5. Trade coverage on 1 Oct 2026 (Chemical Engineering) restates the July 2026 university release. It is not a new experiment.

What the process is

Conventional GO starts with graphite, oxidizes it (Brodie, Staudenmaier, Hummers and variants), then exfoliates. That route needs concentrated acids and leaves a waste stream.

item.title: Holey graphene as a molecular stencil
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported (peer-reviewed method paper). The mid-September 2026 news cycle is a recurrence, not a new isolation of graphene.

Related notes: [[topics/engineering/2026-09-15-ucla-graphene-stencil]] · [[weekly/2026-W38]] · [[recurrence/log]] · [[timeline/2004]]

If you only remember five facts

  1. The method is a mask: graphene covers gold except at engineered holes; thiol-bearing molecules bind gold in the holes and are blocked where intact graphene sits.
  2. The landmark paper is Thomas et al., ACS Nano 9, 10909 (2015), DOI 10.1021/acsnano.5b03936 — “Holey Graphene as a Weed Barrier for Molecules.”
  3. UCLA Health recirculated the same press framing on 14–15 September 2026. Authors named in that release match the 2015 paper (Paul Weiss, John Thomas, Shan Jiang, Nathan Weiss, Xiangfeng Duan, plus Caltech theory from Gethers and Goddard).
  4. Goal stated by the team: patterned nanoelectronic / biosensor surfaces, including devices small enough in principle to think about recording brain-relevant signals. That is a research aim, not a shipped implant.
  5. Graphene here is used for what it blocks (a chemically quiet lid) as much as for what it conducts.

What “stencil” means in this lab

Chemists have long known how to stick molecules to gold. A thiol (–SH) head group binds Au strongly and can form a self-assembled monolayer (SAM). That is a feature and a problem: gold will accept those molecules almost everywhere the surface is clean. If you want a pattern — molecules only in 20-nanometre-class patches, not a uniform film — you need a mask.

item.title: Water dissociation at graphene vacancies
item.description:
Evidence: Preliminary (preprint, simulation)

Machine-learned potentials show solvation changes how water breaks at a graphene single vacancy: competing acidic and basic paths, not the gas-phase concerted path.

Source: arXiv:2609.11602

Evidence: Well-supported for prize, Science FET paper, Nature Nanotechnology 30-inch film, and Nature graphene-on-hBN. Prize lectures are not product warranties.

Prize

5 October 2010: Nobel Prize in Physics to Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov “for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene.” Experiments, not the word, not Wallace, not Boehm. Longer note on the same year: this page is the year entry; the older short Nobel page was merged here.

item.title: 2004 — Isolation at Manchester
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

The experiment, without the myth layer

Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov, and collaborators isolate few-layer and monolayer graphene by mechanical cleavage from graphite — the “Scotch tape” method — transfer flakes onto oxidized silicon, and measure an electric-field effect in atomically thin carbon films.

Landmark: Novoselov et al., Science 306, 666 (2004), “Electric field effect in atomically thin carbon films.”

item.title: 1962 — Boehm monolayers
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported (with later historiographic argument about what “first graphene” means)

What Boehm’s group reported

Hanns-Peter Boehm and colleagues work from graphite oxide, reduce it, and report extremely thin carbon films, including flakes identified as monolayer. The tools are the TEM / diffraction lineage of mid-century surface and colloid carbon chemistry — not a Hall bar on SiO₂.

Geim and Novoselov have publicly pointed at this line as an experimental precursor. The usual careful wording is:

item.title: 1947 — Wallace band structure
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

The paper-shaped object

P. R. Wallace calculates the electronic band structure of a single layer of graphite in order to understand bulk graphite. Near what are now called the Dirac points (the K and K′ corners of the honeycomb Brillouin zone), the bands are linear. Electrons look massless. That linear dispersion is the theoretical signature people now treat as graphene’s calling card.

Wallace is not writing science fiction about sticky tape. He is doing solid-state theory with a two-dimensional unit as the building block of a three-dimensional crystal.

item.title: Science
item.description:
Papers and measurements. Bodies sit on [[topics/medical|Medical]]. Year pages: [[history|History]]. Named papers also: [[reference/key-papers]].

Established enough to teach

  • 2004 isolation and field effect. [[timeline/2004]]
  • 2005 Dirac fermions and quantum Hall. [[timeline/2005]]
  • Copper CVD film, 2009. [[timeline/2009]]
  • GHz FETs, 2010–11 (f_T, not a phone SoC). [[timeline/2010]] · [[timeline/2011]]
  • Dean 2010 hBN encapsulation. [[timeline/2010]]
  • Britnell 2012 vertical FET; Levendorf 2012 lateral hBN. [[timeline/2012]]
  • Furchi 2012 microcavity photodetector. [[timeline/2012]]
  • Nair 2012 GO membranes (helium-tight, water-fast). [[timeline/2012]]
  • Koenig / Bunch 2012 etched-pore sieve. [[timeline/2012]]
  • 2013 waveguide photodetectors. [[timeline/2013]]
  • Liu 2014 double-layer photodetector; Koppens 2014 review; Cai 2014 THz. [[timeline/2014]]
  • Magic-angle bilayer, Cao 2018. [[timeline/2018]]
  • Vocabulary: ISO/TS 80004-13 (2017, 2024) and 21356-1 (2021). [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Did not ship as sold

These were the 2004–12 public pitch. The papers above are real. The products named in that pitch did not arrive as advertised.
